Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Instead, we have had to reconstruct it from fragments scattered through non-Muʿtazilite sources, especially Ashʿarite sources written by some of the Muʿtazila’s fiercest opponents.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
The heritage therefore reaches us in torn pieces, without the unity that originally held it together.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Its internal structure has been lost.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
As researchers, we have also lost the ability to watch the system develop in the complex and logical form in which it originally arose, grew, and changed.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
This makes it extremely difficult to reconstruct a new overall picture that truly matches the logic of the original system.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

If, in the previous two chapters, we have managed to identify a degree of consistency and coherence in the thought of some leading Muʿtazilites, we have done so only by feeling our way along a number of major lines that can still be followed through a record broken and interrupted at many points.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

In our view, the tragedy of the Muʿtazila’s intellectual heritage—the effort of their enemies to erase it—was even more severe than the physical persecution they suffered beginning under the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Indeed, it is more accurate to say that this first tragedy was not theirs alone.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
It was also a tragedy for thought, knowledge, and history.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
We can now ask: why was there such bitter hostility toward the Muʿtazila? And why did they suffer this double tragedy?
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
The rational and liberating character that dominated both the content and method of Muʿtazilite thought was highly progressive when measured against the conditions of their time and society.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

It was this character that brought together a wide range of conservative religious schools, intellectual tendencies, and social groups against them, especially groups whose social position was closely tied to the institutions of the caliphate’s theocratic state.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Among these were, above all, the traditionalists devoted to hadith and many of the jurists.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Despite all the differences between these groups, their opposition to Muʿtazilite rationalism united them on common ground.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
It is true, as we have said before, that Muʿtazilite thought as a whole never left the framework of Islamic ideology. That broad framework was shared by the Muʿtazila and their Ashʿarite opponents.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
But we must still pay attention to what distinguished the Muʿtazila.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
That difference split people who shared the same broad religious ideology into two separate schools: Muʿtazilite and Ashʿarite.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
And these were not simply different schools. They became rival and, in important ways, opposing ones.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
The Muʿtazila’s insistence on reason and on human freedom to act or refrain from acting pushed their thought down a distinctive path.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

As we saw in Chapters Four and Five, this led them to conclusions that objectively turned Muʿtazilite thought into something like a fuse capable of setting off contradictions within the very ideology to which it belonged.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Hostility toward the Muʿtazila was therefore hostility toward these conclusions, because of the cracks they opened within that ideological structure.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
This helps explain why the same wave of hostility eventually spread to science and philosophy as well.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Both the practical sciences and philosophy rely on principles of rational knowledge, even though each uses them in a different way.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Yet history shows that this wave of hostility, violent as it was—and even when it became physically bloody—could not extinguish the spark that Muʿtazilite thought had helped ignite.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
7 — How Did the Rationalist Movement Survive Repression?
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
We can ask the same question in another way.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
How was the movement of rational inquiry, especially in its philosophical form, able to continue developing despite the continuing wave of opposition?
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

One modern scholar explains this by saying that rational inquiry into Islamic doctrine found an organized tool in logic. Logic gave the movement clear theoretical forms and made it difficult to suppress.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
But this explanation does not tell the whole story.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
It is true that the introduction of logic gave the movement greater organization and helped its thinkers express their theories in a more systematic way.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
But logic did not do much more than this formal work. It did not add a new dimension to the movement’s intellectual content, its direction, or the subjects it addressed.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

For that reason, it is hard to believe that formal logic alone gave rational and philosophical thought the strength to survive and continue developing despite the repeated waves of repression directed against it from the persecution of the Muʿtazila down to the age of al-Ghazālī.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

In our view, the source of this resilience—the force that prevented rational inquiry from being swept away by intellectual and physical repression and thrown outside history—was the same force that had brought it into existence in the first place.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
More precisely, it was the continuing development of Arab-Islamic society.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
The development of society had first created the need for rational inquiry among the early Qadarites and later among those who followed them.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
That same social development also created the conditions that allowed the movement to survive and continue.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Indeed, the continued existence and further development of rational inquiry had now become closely connected with the development and progress of society itself.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
This was especially true of cultural development.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
The foundations of cultural life were becoming steadily stronger as social life developed and as the movement of translation and Arabization brought a growing range of foreign cultures into Arabic.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
The social relations created under the caliphate produced increasing interaction between peoples with very different historical backgrounds.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
By this stage, that process had become too powerful for conservative or repressive forces simply to block it.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
We should also remember the political problems created by religious division.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

These divisions demanded arguments about doctrine. And because of the cultural development we have described, those arguments increasingly took a rational form that was historically linked with philosophical thought.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
This reality itself made logical and philosophical thought the leading and most developed form through which people could express the rapidly changing conditions of Abbasid society.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

For all these reasons, the campaign against the Muʿtazila and against the rational and philosophical direction whose earliest foundations they had laid could not destroy that direction or stop its development.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

The hostility directed against it, together with persecution and physical violence, gave new momentum to philosophical thought and won it new supporters across different intellectual and cultural circles, including within the Islamic schools themselves.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
This was especially true among groups whose ideologies stood against the ideology of the caliphate’s theocratic ruling system.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

Ibn Khaldūn makes a statement that is openly sectarian in tone but also contains an implicit historical insight. From it, we can draw a picture that supports what we have said about why rational and philosophical inquiry survived and continued despite growing repression.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

Ibn Khaldūn tries to explain the conditions from which the Muʿtazilite “heresy”—his term for Muʿtazilite thought—emerged. In doing so, he also explains the source of the strength that allowed Muʿtazilite ideas to survive and spread.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
His account suggests that the development of the sciences in their period helped philosophy become widely known and drew people’s attention toward it.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
This created the conditions in which the Muʿtazila could introduce their “heresy” by using philosophy in their arguments.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Their opponents found it difficult to answer them until al-Ashʿarī appeared and began using rational arguments in the same way they did. This allowed him to refute them.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Once the leading Ashʿarites themselves adopted philosophy as a weapon against the Muʿtazila, theologians were able to bring philosophical studies into kalām.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
As Ibn Khaldūn puts it, “From the time of the later theologians onward, philosophy became part of kalām.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Ibn Khaldūn’s account, presented in this way, contains an important historical truth.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Philosophical thought in the age of the Muʿtazila had become a response to real conditions created by the development of culture and by the scientific revival in its many forms.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Philosophy had become an organic part of the inner life of society as a whole.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Formal logic was therefore only one part of the story.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Rational and philosophical inquiry had become powerful enough to impose itself even on some of its most conservative opponents.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

This does not mean, however, that the tragedy of Muʿtazilite thought—which at the same time became a tragedy for philosophy itself—did not obstruct the development of rational thought in the Arab-Islamic world.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
The unfortunate reality is that this tragedy dealt the wider rational movement a serious setback.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Its effects remained visible until the end of that movement’s historical period, when the civilizational role of the Arabs declined in both East and West from the fifteenth century onward.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

Without this setback, the scientific advances already visible in the ninth century suggest that rational and philosophical thought might have moved in a more realistic direction and become more closely connected with the advances being made in the practical sciences of the period.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Instead, beginning with the reign of al-Mutawakkil, a conservative traditionalist wave became dominant.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
The historian al-Masʿūdī describes the change in these words:
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

“When the caliphate passed to al-Mutawakkil, he ordered people to abandon speculative debate and to leave behind the practices that had prevailed under al-Muʿtaṣim and al-Wāthiq. He ordered people to submit and follow established authority, and he instructed the leading hadith scholars to teach hadith and openly promote the Sunna and the community.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

“Although he [al-Mutawakkil] was one of the most unjust of the caliphs, the people of the Sunna praised him and overlooked his wrongdoing because he ended the miḥna”—that is, the period of Muʿtazilite dominance. “Many hadith scholars even reported dreams in which they were told that God had forgiven him.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Al-Suyūṭī, discussing the same subject, says that al-Mutawakkil:
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
“…brought the hadith scholars to Samarra”—his capital—“gave them generous gifts, honored them, and ordered them to teach the traditions concerning the divine attributes and the vision of God.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
These were two questions that the Muʿtazila rejected.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

“Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shayba sat in the mosque of al-Ruṣāfa, and around thirty thousand people gathered around him. His brother sat in the mosque of al-Manṣūr, and around thirty thousand gathered around him. The people prayed abundantly for al-Mutawakkil and went to great lengths in praising and honoring him.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

Then al-Mutawakkil ordered his governor in Egypt to shave the beard of Egypt’s chief judge, Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Abī al-Layth, who was a Muʿtazilite, have him beaten, and parade him through the streets on a donkey.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
He then replaced him as judge with al-Ḥārith ibn Miskīn, a follower of Mālik.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

The Mālikī school to which al-Ḥārith ibn Miskīn belonged was, as is well known, among the legal schools most firmly attached to the traditionalist approach. It relied very heavily on hadith and was among those most strongly opposed to rational inquiry in matters of religious doctrine and law.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
This helps us understand the meaning of the return, under al-Mutawakkil, to the dominance of this earlier traditionalist tendency after the Muʿtazila suffered their political defeat at his hands.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
It was therefore a reactionary response to the Muʿtazilite movement, which had firmly established the role of reason not only in questions of religious belief, but also in Islamic law.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

Historically, the Muʿtazila had made a clear distinction between these two fields: belief and law. From the third Islamic century onward, they separated the subjects of kalām—the study of religious beliefs—from those of fiqh, the study of Islamic law. Before that, “all the major books of kalām recognized by most Muslims had dealt with some questions of jurisprudence as well.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

The Muʿtazila thus became “the first Islamic school to free itself from all the tendencies of the jurists, and the only purely theological school” among the five major groups into which Muslims were then divided: the Sunnis, Muʿtazila, Murjiʾa, Shiʿa, and Kharijites. They held that every qualified scholar who exercised independent judgment could arrive at a valid answer in questions of law. Muʿtazilites could therefore be found in every school of jurisprudence, “even among the scholars of Hadith, who are usually regarded as the fiercest enemies of the theologians.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

This fact about the Muʿtazila gives us further evidence of the deep influence their thinking had on the intellectual life of their age. They helped direct it toward rational inquiry and, later, toward philosophy in particular. Their influence was so strong and so deeply rooted that successive waves of hostility toward reason and rational knowledge could not wipe it out.

Scientific method points us toward an important fact in the history of human societies and civilizations: when gradual quantitative changes build up over time, their eventual transformation into something qualitatively new can take many different forms.
The result may be political, social, or intellectual. It may take the form of a new theoretical outlook, or it may erupt as revolutionary violence.

Engels studied the different forms taken by revolutionary opposition to medieval feudalism. He found that, depending on the historical conditions, this opposition appeared at one time as mysticism, at another as open heresy, and at another as armed revolt.

The particular form taken by a qualitative transformation in any society and at any time is determined by the concrete conditions of real life. Sometimes those conditions may be ripe for several kinds of transformation at once. Political, social, and intellectual changes may all occur together. They may be accompanied by armed uprisings, they may prepare the way for them, or development may proceed without revolutionary violence at all.

This idea helps us understand the long process of accumulation in Arab-Islamic society during the seventh and eighth centuries, a process whose most representative intellectual transformation was kalām.
